694.title: Where it didn't
694.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often review honestly where it hasn't helped, and many pair it with other support, such as friends, counseling, rest or a faith community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it worked. Your line was it worked here. Did you write down the moment you found, with the day or the place? Keep it close. Today we turn it over. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Three in the morning. You know all the lines by now. Some things are up to us, some aren't. It isn't the thing, it's your judgment about the thing. You could recite them in your sleep, if you could sleep. And none of it is touching the knot in your chest. The words sit there like a poster on a waiting room wall. Everyone who has practiced anything for a year has a night like that. Yesterday we named where the porch helped. Today, just as plainly: where it didn't.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `ALL THE LINES, NO SLEEP.` → `WHERE IT DIDN'T HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics saw this coming. In the Discourses, Epictetus challenges his students: show me a Stoic, if you can. Not someone who can talk Stoic, but someone who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. He says he'd gladly see one, and implies he hasn't. Seneca, in his essay On the Happy Life, imagines critics saying he talks one way and lives another. He doesn't deny it. He says he isn't wise, that he speaks about virtue, not about himself, and that he is still fighting his own faults. The teachers didn't claim the method always worked on them. Second, where it can misfire. When it turns into small-s stoic: teeth gritted, feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. When up to us and not up to us becomes an excuse to shrug at something you could change, or something unfair that someone should challenge. And when the trouble is depression, a deep loss, or a body that needs care. A maxim is not a doctor, a friend, or a night's sleep. Third, two honest reasons. Sometimes the tool was fine and you were hungry, exhausted, or alone. Sometimes the tool was the wrong one for the job. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a failure of character. Fourth, why say it out loud. A practice that only reports its wins turns into a sales pitch. One that can say here, it didn't help stays a practice, something you use with open eyes. Marcus's notebook is full of the same honesty: you're doing it again, start over.
screen: `SHOW ME A STOIC, IF YOU CAN.` · `WHERE IT CAN MISFIRE.` · `TIRED, OR THE WRONG TOOL.` · `HONESTY KEEPS IT A PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HONEST ABOUT IT.`

segments.voice: Let one moment come where the porch didn't help. Choose one you can look at today; you don't have to open the heaviest one. Where were you? What did you reach for, and what happened? Then ask, gently: was I tired, hungry, alone? Or was this the wrong tool? Don't judge the answer. Just name it. If what comes up is heavy and still with you, that's a reason to talk to someone you trust, not to try harder alone. The bell holds the time.
Where it didn't: an honest look at one moment when Stoic practice didn't help, and why, without blame. Today's word.

Your line: honest about it. Next to yesterday's moment, write today's, in one sentence. Then add one thing that might help next time, whether it's sleep, a person, or a different tool. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: Ahead: the great questions
695.hook: year three turns to suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, across many traditions
695.howItsDone: Many people on their own spiritual path return again and again to a few great questions, reading what different traditions, philosophers and scientists say about each.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it didn't. Your line was honest about it. Did you write the moment down, next to the one where it worked, with one thing that might help next time? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Some questions come up at four in the afternoon, between emails. Most don't. The big ones come in hospital corridors, at gravesides, on the night a baby is born, in the car after you've been let go, on a mountain when the clouds suddenly open. Why is there so much suffering? What happens when we die? Can I forgive this? Traditions all over the world have sat up late with those questions. Tomorrow the porch closes for the year. Today we look ahead.
screen: `HOSPITAL CORRIDORS, MOUNTAINTOPS.` → `THE QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `TODAY, WE LOOK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the six. Year three is built around six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, and awe. Not a new school this time, and not a single book. Six themes, each given room, one after another. Second, how it works. For each question, we'll hear many voices: scripture and saints, sages and poets, philosophers and scientists. Every voice is named. A line from the Psalms is the Psalms; a teaching of the Buddha is the Buddha's; a finding from a lab is the lab's. Nobody is blended into anybody else, and nobody is ranked. Where traditions see a question differently, and on death they really do, we say who says what, in their own words, and leave it there. Third, the porch comes too. The Stoics don't disappear. On death we've already sat with Marcus and the ripe olive that falls blessing the tree; on awe, with Marcus again, looking down from above. In year three they take a seat at a much bigger table, one voice among many. Fourth, questions to live with. In 1903 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who had asked him for advice. Be patient, he told him, with what is still unsettled in you. Love the questions themselves. Don't chase answers you aren't ready to live yet. Live the questions now, and one day you may find, almost without noticing, that you've grown into an answer. That's the spirit of year three. Not a quiz with answers in the back. A year of keeping good company with the hardest questions there are.
screen: `SIX QUESTIONS, ONE AT A TIME.` · `MANY VOICES, EACH ONE NAMED.` · `THE STOICS AT A BIGGER TABLE.` · `LOVE THE QUESTIONS THEMSELVES.` · then, large: `THE BIG QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Let the six questions pass through you, one breath each. Suffering. Death. Love. Work. Forgiveness. Awe. Don't think hard about any of them. Just notice which one tugs, which one your body leans toward, or flinches from. That's often the one. When you've found it, let it stay. You don't need an answer. Just let the question sit beside you, like a companion for the road. The bell holds the time.
Ahead: year three, six great questions, suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, heard through many named voices. Today's word.
Your line: the big questions. Write the one you picked at the top of a fresh page, and leave the rest of the page blank. It's for year three to fill. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the porch
696.hook: the school of the porch is yours to visit any time
696.howItsDone: Many people who study the Stoics keep returning to a handful of texts, the Handbook, Seneca's letters and the Meditations, rereading them over the years as guides rather than rulebooks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahead, to the big questions. Your line was the big questions. Did you write yours at the top of a blank page? Leave it there. Day six hundred ninety-six. The last day of year two.

A porch is a strange kind of room. It has a roof, so you can shelter there. It has no front wall, so the street comes right up to it. People stop on the steps to talk, to wait out the rain, to watch the evening come in. Nobody checks a ticket. You can stay an hour or a minute, and come back whenever you like. Around three hundred years before the common era, a school of philosophy started on exactly that kind of porch. We have spent a whole year sitting on it. Today we close year two.
screen: `A ROOF, BUT NO FRONT WALL.` → `NOBODY CHECKS A TICKET.` → `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: First, the porch itself. In Athens, on the edge of the marketplace, stood a long covered colonnade with famous paintings on its walls, the Painted Porch, the Stoa Poikile. Zeno of Citium taught there, in public, where anyone passing could stop and listen. His students were called the people of the stoa: Stoics. The name of the school is the name of a porch. Second, the year, room by room. We opened with Epictetus's Handbook, in order: some things are up to us, some are not. Then his Discourses, the talks his student Arrian wrote down. Then Seneca, his letters to Lucilius and his essays, flawed and kind. Then the Meditations, all twelve books, straight through, an emperor's notebook to himself. And last, the wider porch: the founders, the neighbors next door, the turning year, and the porch lived at work, at home, in grief and in love. This last week we kept three habits, let one go, thanked three teachers, and said honestly where it worked and where it didn't. Third, guides, not masters. Seneca writes to Lucilius that the thinkers who came before us are not our masters but our guides. The truth, he says, lies open to everyone, and nobody has taken possession of it yet. That's how he read his own school, and it's a good way to leave it. Fourth, the porch stays open. A porch has no door to lock behind you. Whatever you kept from this year, a morning intention, an evening question, a delayed reply, you can step back up onto it any day you want. Tomorrow, year three: six questions.
screen: `THE PAINTED PORCH IN ATHENS.` · `A YEAR, ROOM BY ROOM.` · `GUIDES, NOT MASTERS.` · `A PORCH HAS NO DOOR TO LOCK.` · then, large: `THE PORCH STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Find a step, if you can: a porch, a stoop, a front step, a stair in your building. Or sit in a doorway, half in and half out. Sit down. Feel the roof or the sky above you, and the open side in front. Let the year come to you as one picture: whichever teacher, line or moment stayed. Don't sort it or grade it. Just sit with it, the way people have always sat on steps at the end of the day. The bell holds the time.
Year two close: the end of a year with the Stoics, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, on a porch with no door, open whenever you return. Today's word, and the last of year two.
Your line: the porch stays open. Choose one Stoic habit to carry into year three, and do it once more tonight. Then rest. Tomorrow, six questions. Day six hundred ninety-six.
